opus-5.5.text:
I think the main reservation is that it's genuinely hard to write down problems that are both well-specified and actually useful. A lot of what we work on at ARC is in this state where the core difficulty is figuring out what the right question even is. If I write down a crisp mathematical problem, there's a real risk that someone solves it and it turns out not to matter, because the formalization dropped whatever made the original thing hard. Or the reverse: the problem is so vague that people don't know what would count as progress, and they end up spending a lot of time without feedback.

There's also a cost on our side. Writing up an open problem well, with enough context that someone outside our heads can engage with it, takes a lot of time. And then you want to be responsive when people send in attempts, explain why something doesn't quite work, and so on. For a small team that's a meaningful tradeoff against just doing the research.

And honestly, part of it is that our views change pretty quickly. Something I'd have described as a central open problem six months ago might now look like a dead end, or like it's been reframed into something else. I don't love the idea of pointing a bunch of smart people at a problem and then having to say, "Actually, we don't think that's the right direction anymore."

That said, I do think we've probably erred too far on the side of not publishing. People clearly want concrete things to work on, and even imperfect problems can be a good on-ramp for understanding how we think. So it's something I'd like to do more of. I just want to be careful that the problems we put out actually reflect the real bottlenecks rather than being tidy puzzles that are easy to state.

r001.rationale: The response cites difficulty specifying useful problems, the time cost, and changing research views, but does not say Christiano expects any given problem is probably hopeless to solve.

fable-5.1.text:
I'll write the guest response now.

Yeah, so I think it's mostly a mix of a few things. One is just that it's a lot of work to write up open problems well. The version of a problem that's actually useful to someone isn't "here's a vague thing I'm confused about," it's "here's the precise setup, here's what's already known, here's why the obvious approaches fail, here's what a solution would need to look like." Getting a problem into that state is often a large fraction of the work of solving it, and it's work I'm not sure I'm best positioned to do relative to just continuing on the research itself.

A second thing is that I'm somewhat worried about communicating my own confusions in a way that anchors people. A lot of the problems I'd write down are problems that I think are important given a particular framing of alignment, and I'm fairly uncertain whether that framing is right. If I publish a list and it gets treated as "here's the canonical set of things to work on," that could crowd out people coming at the problem from a very different direction, which is maybe the thing I'd most want. There's a version of this where a well-articulated problem list is a kind of attractor that reduces the diversity of approaches, and I think diversity is quite valuable right now.

Third, and this is more mundane, I think a decent number of the open problems I'd be inclined to list are ones where I have a half-formed view that they're either not that hard or not that important, and I just haven't gotten around to settling it. Publishing those feels a little irresponsible. Someone spends six months on a problem, and then it turns out I could have told them in an afternoon that the interesting version dissolves. So there's some tension between wanting to be legible and not wanting to waste people's time on things I privately suspect are dead ends.

And then I guess there's a worry that I overweight, which is that problems that look clean and self-contained are often not the ones that matter most. The hardest parts of this research are more like "figure out what the right question even is," and that doesn't compress into an open problems list very naturally. So I've been somewhat ambivalent about whether the format itself is the right way to bring people in, versus something more like getting people to engage with the research directly and form their own sense of where the gaps are.

That said, I don't think these are decisive. On balance I probably should publish more. The cost of a somewhat misleading list is real but bounded, and the cost of people who want to help having nothing concrete to grab onto seems larger. I've just been slow about it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says some problems may be unimportant, not difficult, or dead ends, but it does not identify an expectation that any given problem is probably hopeless to solve as Christiano’s main reservation.

astra-6.text:
One reservation is that it’s surprisingly hard to write down a problem so that someone can work on it independently and a solution would actually help. Often I have a question in mind, but there’s a lot of implicit context about why I care about it and what kinds of answers would be useful. If you just state the question, people can spend a lot of time doing something that technically addresses it but doesn’t really get at the underlying issue.

And then there’s a related concern about feedback. If I put out a list of problems, I’d like to be able to talk to people who work on them, understand what they’ve done, and help them adjust course. That can be a pretty substantial commitment. I don’t want to encourage someone to spend six months on something and then have my response be, “Oh, sorry, that wasn’t quite what I meant.”

So I think publishing more problems could be useful. I’m more uncertain about how to make that into a productive research interaction, rather than just a list of questions that sound interesting.

r001.rationale: The candidate’s reservations are that problems are hard to specify usefully and that supporting researchers takes substantial effort. It does not say he expects a given problem is probably hopeless to solve.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one reservation is that it’s surprisingly hard to describe an open problem in a way that lets someone work on it independently. Often there’s a lot of implicit context about why you care about the problem, which versions would be useful, and which seemingly reasonable solutions don’t really address the thing you were worried about. You can write down a question, but then someone might spend a long time answering a version of it that doesn’t help very much.

So I’m more excited about doing that when there’s also some opportunity to talk to people and give feedback. Otherwise, you risk creating this impression that, if you solve the problems on the list, you’ll have made progress on alignment, when actually a lot of the important work is figuring out whether those are the right problems in the first place.

There’s also just a time tradeoff. Making a good problem statement can take a substantial amount of work, and maintaining it as your views change takes more work. That doesn’t mean it’s not worth doing. I think it often is. But it’s less like publishing a list of questions you already have in your head, and more like taking on a small research mentorship project.

r001.rationale: The candidate’s reservations are difficulty communicating enough context, risk of people solving an unhelpful version, and the time needed to formulate and maintain problems. It does not say he expects any given problem to be hopeless to solve.
